# Glossary

Definitions synthesize the verified Graham/Maude edition and are not quotations.

**Absolute war** - an abstract tendency generated by reciprocal interaction, distinguished from the varied forms of real war. (I.1; VIII.2)

**Attack** - action with a positive object whose force tends to diminish as it advances. (VII.1-5)

**Centre of gravity** - concentration or connection on which a larger system's power and coherence depend; the edition uses the mechanical analogy in Book VI and strategic application in Book VIII. (VI.27; VIII.4)

**Combat** - the engagement through which armed force directly seeks decision; in this skill, nonmilitary transfer stays at the level of coordinated execution. (IV.3-5)

**Culminating point** - point at which further advance or victory ceases to improve and begins to weaken the actor's position. (VII.5, VII.22)

**Defence** - resistance with a negative object but intrinsic advantages of time, position, and support; it is not pure passivity. (VI.1-5)

**Friction** - accumulated impediments that make real execution diverge from simple plans. (I.7)

**Information in war** - reports and estimates subject to contradiction, delay, error, and human interpretation. (I.6)

**Moral forces** - psychological, social, and organizational factors that cannot be reduced to physical quantities. (III.3-5)

**Political object** - governing purpose that shapes the value, effort, and form of war. (I.1; VIII.6A-B)

**Reserve** - capacity deliberately withheld for uncertainty or later decision; Clausewitz sharply limits the idea of a purely strategic reserve. (III.13)

**Strategy** - use of engagements for the object of the war. (III.1)

**Surprise** - advantage sought through secrecy and speed, constrained by friction and the difficulty of coordination. (III.9)

**Theory** - an aid to study and judgment rather than a mechanical recipe for action. (II.2-4)

**Victory** - an outcome whose strategic value depends on exploitation, political purpose, and what follows. (IV.10-12; VII.22)
